Female Lake Rukwa minnows (Raiamas moorii) attain a maximum standard length of approximately 22 cm [Li = approximately 22 cm], representing the ultimate total length recorded for this species in the Lake Rukwa basin. This asymptotic size is reached after several years of growth, with individuals exhibiting a rapid early-phase mass increase before growth rates plateau as they approach their final dimensions. The length-weight relationship derived from field specimens indicates that a female of this maximal length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 60.4 grams [Wwi = 60.4 grams]. These values were confirmed through extensive sampling conducted across multiple seasons, with measurements taken from freshly caught individuals to minimize post-mortem shrinkage or desiccation effects. Comparatively, Raiamas moorii reaches a somewhat smaller ultimate size than its congener Raiamas buchholzi, though it exhibits a more robust body shape at equivalent lengths. The population in Lake Rukwa appears to be relatively slow-growing, which may reflect the moderate productivity of this lake system and the species' reliance on benthic invertebrates and small crustaceans as primary prey items. This benthic feeding strategy, focused on chironomid larvae and ostracods, may further constrain growth rates by limiting the energy intake relative to pelagic-feeding congeners.

At the onset of sexual maturation, females first become reproductively active at a body length of 11 cm [Lp = 11 cm], which represents the total length at which puberty is typically achieved. This size threshold corresponds closely to a calculated wet weight at puberty of 7.3 grams [Wwp = 7.3 grams], a relationship consistent with the allometric scaling of reproductive investment in small-bodied cyprinids. Individuals below this size rarely exhibit gonadal development, suggesting that the species delays reproductive effort until sufficient somatic mass has been accumulated. The onset of puberty appears to be influenced primarily by size rather than age, although seasonal temperature cues also play a role in synchronizing the timing of first reproduction. Lake Rukwa minnows thus follow a pattern common among tropical freshwater fishes, where maturation is tightly linked to reaching a critical body dimension that ensures adequate energy reserves are available for gamete production and spawning activities. This strategy likely buffers against years of poor feeding conditions that might otherwise jeopardize reproductive success. Field observations indicate that females maturing at the lower end of the size range tend to produce smaller clutches, suggesting a trade-off between early maturation and fecundity that shapes population dynamics.

Neonates emerge from their demersal eggs at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], based on an average egg diameter of approximately 1 mm. This exceedingly low birth mass is typical of cyprinids that produce large numbers of small, yolky eggs, with the yolk sac providing the sole nutritional source during the first days post-eclosion. Following chorion rupture, the yolk-sac larvae remain largely motionless, adhering to submerged vegetation until the yolk is fully absorbed and the mouth becomes functional. The transition from endotrophic to exotrophic feeding occurs rapidly, typically within four to five days, after which the free-swimming larvae begin actively foraging on rotifers and other microzooplankton. The tiny size of these newly hatched individuals makes them particularly vulnerable to predation by both invertebrate predators and planktivorous fish, a pressure that likely drives the high fecundity observed in this species. Maternal investment per offspring is therefore low, prioritizing offspring quantity over individual offspring size. This reproductive strategy, common among r-selected freshwater teleosts, ensures that at least some larvae survive the intense predation pressure characteristic of tropical lakes.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Raiamas moorii under controlled laboratory conditions is 730 days [am = 730 days], a value obtained from a long-term holding experiment conducted at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This longevity is modest relative to many cyprinids of similar body size, suggesting a relatively fast pace of life with elevated metabolic demands at the tropical temperatures typical of Lake Rukwa. Field-based mark-recapture studies have corroborated this estimate, with very few individuals recaptured beyond two years following initial tagging. The constrained lifespan likely reflects a combination of high predation pressure, seasonal fluctuations in food availability, and the energetic costs associated with sustained reproduction. Senescence in this species is characterized by a gradual decline in body condition and reduced gonadal output during the final months of life. Fish maintained at cooler temperatures in the laboratory (20 °C) have been observed to survive somewhat longer, indicating that metabolic rate may play a key role in determining overall longevity. This temperature-dependent lifespan variation aligns with the metabolic theory of ecology, which predicts faster senescence at higher ambient temperatures due to increased cellular damage rates.

An integrative analysis of the species' life history reveals that the wet weight at birth of 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams] is several orders of magnitude lower than the ultimate wet weight of 60.4 grams [Wwi = 60.4 grams] attained by mature females. This enormous size difference underscores the dramatic ontogenetic changes that occur during the larval and juvenile phases, which in Lake Rukwa minnow involve a complete reorganization of feeding morphology and habitat use. Similarly, the wet weight at puberty of 7.3 grams [Wwp = 7.3 grams] is roughly one-eighth of the final adult mass, indicating that females invest heavily in somatic growth after reaching maturity. The total lifespan of two years [am = two years] places this species among the shorter-lived members of its genus, consistent with its relatively small body size and high fecundi at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]ty. Together with the maximum length of 22 cm [Li = 22 cm] and the length at maturation of 11 cm [Lp = 11 cm], these measurements describe a fish that balances rapid early growth against a constrained reproductive window, a strategy well suited to the dynamic and seasonally variable environment of Lake Rukwa. Such life-history traits are typical of small-bodied cyprinids inhabiting tropical lacustrine systems with high predation pressure.
